utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours will recall last week --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. I promised to get the war diary from Mr. Tomanovic, if you remember, the one we were discussing the last day of business, and I have now here everything that Mr. Tomanovic himself had. I have a copy for myself and I can provide two copies for Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would the usher please collect the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to stress that this is not the diary in its entirety and that Mr. Tomanovic has made a formal request to be provided with the integral diary. However, even in what we have here, the incomplete one, you will find the critical dates that Mr. Nice was interested in; that is to say the 27th of April, and mention is made there of the anti-terrorist operation that we talked about. So the portions he was interested in are to be found in the portions that I have provided. As to the diary in its entirety, a request has been put in to receive that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Let it be passed to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We were informed last week, after the close of Court proceedings, as to how it came about that documents were in the somewhat confused format that they were in Your Honour's exhibit, and I have no reason to doubt the accuracy of what Ms. Dicklich was told by one of the accused's associates, and that is that the material that was available in the original format, that is to say an actual diary extract, was in part transcribed for legibility for the accused, thus the passages in the exhibit that are in Cyrillic, typed Cyrillic, because he, like the rest of us - there is no reason to doubt this, of course - can have difficulty reading somebody else's handwriting. So there's nothing sinister in that, that just explains that. There was then translation in part of the original from the Cyrillic typed transcript, it matters not which, into English, and that's what we had available for ourselves. Now, as to the -- what the accused says about the 27th and 28th, I'll just look to that now myself. Oh, and I should say as well, I gather -- I gather from Ms. Dicklich and via the accused's representative that CLSS declines to translate documents of a certain category, and I think this may be one of them. Handwritten documents of this kind. And again, there is no reason to doubt what the accused said about that. So none of the things that I was raising last week necessarily can be held against him at all, and I ought to make that clear. Having said that, I'll tell you what I can now see. Of course, if this had come to us earlier -- I make no complaint, yesterday was a UN holiday, but these documents are potentially very important or very valuable. What had been produced then by way of a selection for us in tab 6 simply started at the 24th of March. That appears to be the same. So there's no addition to what Your Honours have got there. I had wondered, incidentally, when contemplating if more material would be forthcoming, whether it would be prudent for me to seek an adjournment so as not to consume my limited time in an exercise like this, but I suspect that the process of organising such an adjournment would consume more time than will be taken by doing it in your presence. So the first pages in the original that you have are provided for us here, and there is no expansion on that. There are then original handwritten pages in a different format for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd of April, and the Court will, I possibly recall, that there were some typed up English pages from the 4th of April onwards. So the 1st, 2nd and 3rd, I think, would appear to be new, and I'll have those looked at in a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we are of the view that you should take the break to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's very kind. I'm almost done. We then have -- I'm just telling you -- I'm happy to take a break to do it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, take the break. Well, I was hoping to conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: By that time. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that's one of the problems. And I'm very anxious not to break any time limits. There are then other handwritten pages, and there does then appear to be a series of pages that runs from the 25th of April through to the 28th. The format again is slightly different, and there are odd days. I'll simply ask that they may be reviewed now by my team members, and I'll come back to it either before the break or, if necessary, shortly afterwards, but there does seem to be some additional material coming from the accused's papers in the way that he's described to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I didn't follow the part where you said that CLSS decline to translate the handwritten documents. Why is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not for me to explain CLSS's practices nor indeed even by implication to criticise them. I suspect the point is that if CLSS is given a substantial handwritten document, the consumption of resources for that is -- yes. They won't do a full document that is handwritten or what is a substantial document that's handwritten, and although I don't know, I guess that is because the consumption of resources by both deciphering and translating is so much greater than for other documents that in the balance of priorities, they make a decision against that type of document. But that's a matter for them. It is, I think, a policy we've known of now for some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If penmanship is no better than mine, then one could understand the difficulty that they would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djosan, just before we turn from the issue of the war diary that's been touched on, is it your understanding of the way things worked with the VJ Commission for Cooperation that they decided what documents would be provided either to you directly or to the accused's associates?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't enter into the methods of work practiced by the commission. And as I've already said or, rather, said a few days ago, the commission called me up and showed me the written text in the book mentioned and asked me to give my statements pertaining to certain events, and that was sufficient for me. As to the methods they applied, I really could not go into that nor did I have any need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to recap to this extent: Events that you have described in your statements to the VJ commission were covered by contemporaneous documents held now in archives; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you seek, and if you did seek were you allowed to see, any of those documents before making your statements to the VJ commission?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're sure about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you accept that of course contemporaneous documents are the most valuable for people like judges dealing with events of several years ago?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my conviction that the most valuable documents are those which came into being at the time the events took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Contemporaneous documents.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Events -- yes, yes. If you -- if that is what you like to call it, contemporaneous, yes; I say the specific time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was any reason given to you by the VJ commission for its acting as a filter between providing original documents frequently requested by the Office of the Prosecutor and this Court? Was any reason given why they acted as a filter in the way they did?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, they did not filter as far as I could see, and I had no reason to give it a second thought. They gave me no pretext, no reason for me to make conclusions of that kind. They called me up, they said, "General, take a look at what is written here. Please write a statement referring to those concrete events."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's look at tab 7 in your exhibits, if you'd be so good, please. Example. You said -- before we look at it, the two purposes which I have, you said to us this morning at -- they called you up and they showed you the written text in the book mentioned, that is "As Seen, As Told." Just remind us: Did you or did you not read the book yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read parts, the parts which relate to the concrete events they asked me about, but I haven't read the book in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have any doubts as to whose work it was, that book, that it was the work of the OSCE, or did you think that it was the work of Natasa Kandic herself?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To this day I have reason to doubt the book, because I do not know who the authors of the book are. Who was it who saw what he wrote about? It's one thing to publish a book. It's another thing to write the book, and it's a third thing again to see something and then say it. "As Seen, As Told" brings into doubt or, rather, requires and demands that we see who it is who did the seeing and did the telling. Who published it is of lesser importance. And I personally would like you to give me the name of one of the authors, the ones that saw it and then told it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Djosan, don't worry, we've heard in this Court from the person who compiled this book, with a full account of its methodology, but more than that, let's go, please, if we can, to the second page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think that's the point the witness is making, Mr. Nice. The point he's making is that the real authors of the book are the people who gave the information to the people who compiled it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand that and it's to that that I'm now turning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go, please, to the second page of your statement and the penultimate paragraph, you say this in English translation: "I have read the information that the forces of the FRY allegedly took part in the destruction of those parts of the town in a book published by the Humanitarian Law Centre, "Kosovo: As Seen, As Told." Can you tell us, please, which page you're referring to and which paragraph in the book.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I state again: I don't have the book before me and I don't remember all the quotations from the book exactly, but I would like to hear who it was who saw. You didn't tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who saw it and who told it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... repeat. You're here to give evidence of events and you set out in a statement that you've read something and that you challenge it. Now, you must know, as a man of intelligence and education, that if you want to challenge something, we need chapters and verse. I was pursuing the line of His Honour Judge Bonomy before he raised the matter that he did: If you can tell me the page and paragraph number, I can show you how this book is footnoted by references not to named witnesses necessarily but to witnesses. Were you aware of that, that this book is always footnoted to the existence of, the number of, and the pseudonyms of witnesses? Were you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote here about a concrete event. I wasn't responding and answering to footnotes from --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the book named.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please listen to the question. You have complained about the lack of authorship of this book. Here is a passage in a statement you want this Court to rely upon as valuable evidence. I'm asking you, please tell me, which passage of the book are you referring to, and I'll then enable you to join issue with the authors. Can you tell us the passage, please, Mr. Djosan? Because if you can't, we can't deal with this assertion of yours. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tell you again: I wrote a statement about an event which relates to the 24th of March, 1999, based on my recollections and knowledge, that is to say the knowledge and recollections of myself and my subordinates and superiors. Now, had I known that you had wanted me to address every footnote and every detail, then I would know how to respond. But what was asked of me was to provide my own descriptions of the event based on my own knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... question. Since you make a reference to footnotes, please pick up this part of my question: In saying what you said in this statement about "As Seen, As Told" and in saying what you said to this Court what you said about authorship of the accounts in "As Seen, As Told," were you aware or not at the time that this was a footnoted book, identifying sources? Because the way you've written your statement doesn't make that apparent, does it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to tell you and I'll try once again. I did not comment or reply to the person writing the footnotes. What I did was to provide the commission with my own statement, which I signed and which I stand by, and I think that that is sufficient for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'd like to hear the footnote that you're referring to. Who is the author of that particular footnote?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Djosan, you will recall I've asked you for the page reference and the paragraph reference to what you say you've read in the book and you can't give it, and I'm going to suggest to you that in fact what happened was that the VJ commission probably summarised in the most general terms what they said was in this book and they then asked you to write statements. And the reason I suggest that includes what we've seen in Vukovic with his ridiculous statements about not being able to read on further in the book because he was so disgusted by Natasa Kandic. Is that what happened, they just said, "This is what the book says, and it's Natasa Kandic's book"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you're not right. You're not right. The commission did not tell us about the book. I had the book in my own house for two days and leafed through it and the part relating to Djakovica. It never entered my mind to enter into polemics with somebody who has a name or surname or pseudonym as the writer of the footnotes. I described what I saw based on the knowledge I had. Now, what Mr. Vukovic wrote, well, it's his right to like somebody or not like somebody. I don't want to pursue that point further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first page now of this same statement, please. And we'll just have a look at what you've said so far about in the way of detail. If we look halfway down the first page in your version, and a little bit further in the English version, there's a paragraph that goes as follows: "On the night when the NATO aggression started --" it's on the overhead projector. "On the night when the NATO aggression started, I was at Cabrat hill near Djakovica. The brigade operations centre was located at the foot of the hill. The logistics battalion was in the town of Djakovica, deployed by element and organisational units. The command battalion was located on the outskirts of town at the foot of Cabrat. In the courtyard Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of a house owned by the Marsenic family we had shelters for personnel and the weapons we had set up earlier on the hill, but we moved our P-15 radars we were using to monitor the airspace from that location to other ones. We expected that our area would be targeted by NATO planes in the first moments of NATO aggression." Then the next paragraph: "The first target to be struck by cruise missiles was Devet Jugovica barracks, where the forward command post of the Pristina Corps was located..." Right. Just help me: All of that from memory, was it, or do you have any form of note to which you wish to refer?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote all that from memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... did you, and by now a general or retired general, that in November 2002 it was a safe and satisfactory thing to do, to record events of three and a half years before to do it all from memory?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such events stay etched in your memory for a long time. The beginning and the end of the war remain in your memory very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, there are no times in that and there are no particular names apart from one name of one family, so let's go to tab 10, please. Now, tab 10 is another of your statements, this time made on the 27th of December, 2002. This is a statement about activities on the 1st of April, 1999. And if we go down to the -- the paragraph following the deployment of forces -- I suppose we might as well look at that. Are you able to remember that the 1st PVO was in the Kijevo and the 2nd in Gnjilane, and the 3rd in the Djakovica sector and so on? Were you able to remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had been there since the 9th. That part of my statement is a preamble. They had been there from the 9th April onwards. So at the time, they were still in the area of Djakovica. You were able to see in all my statements that they always begin with a preamble, the introductory part dealing with my duties, when I assumed them, how I performed them, et cetera. So on that date in April, my units were not in Gracanica, in Bec, or Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at the next paragraph: "In addition to the above units, there was a rocket battery with a KUB-M missile system from the strength of the 311th Pristina Self-propelled Rocket Regiment settlement in the general area of Bec. At about 2230 hours on the 31st of March ... two NATO aeroplanes approached ..." Well, this is a modest three and a half years -- modest three and a half years later. Where do you get the time from?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time was indicated exactly because I was there at that moment. I was directly involved and I was saving those soldiers. Of course I remember such an important event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Didn't even want to check. You didn't think, as a person knowing your evidence would be in court, well, I think it's about 10.00, or I think it's 10.30, but I want to check. No, happy just to do it from memory. Although the documents that could prove all this, documents that the OTP in general if not specifically, I simply don't know, had thought are sitting in an archive waiting for you to review them, yes? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was absolutely no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Nor any desire on your part, as a military man, to check records.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning such an event where my own soldiers were killed, I didn't need to go to the archives to check when and how they died. Plus there were so many people that -- who talked to me, including Vukasinovic, whose statement you also have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you mean, talked to you in the commission and shared their recollections rather than going back to the records? Did no one want to go back to the records? Did no one put their hand up to the commission meeting and say, "Please, can we see our documents?" Did nobody do that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about other people. Please ask me questions concerning myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a meeting of people with the commission, telling you what you were going to be doing in preparing material that this Court is being invited to act on as reliable, or were you dealt with one-to-one? Were you brought into an office and told, "Do this," or were you spoken to generally at a big meeting? You just tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was called and told, "General, please look at this book, see what it says, and please write a statement about this event." They did not try to influence me as to what I would write or how I would write it. They just said, "Please bring us your statement. You know that you must be responsible for it in a moral sense and legal sense." They did not tell me what to write and how. And whatever is written here I am prepared to stand by, otherwise I would never have written it in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you write this statement then and there or did you take some time to consider it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wrote the statement in my office. At that time, I was on what is called stand-by, on call. I still had the right to go to work, to come and use my office when I needed to. And before that, I rang up my superior, Colonel Vukasinovic, from whose units the soldiers were. But I was personally on the spot when this stopped. I was saving those soldiers from under fire. I and Lieutenant Colonel Drago Milic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Djosan, you say that the request you received from the commission was to write about this event. Can you tell me the language that was used in describing this event when you got your request from the commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what you mean by "language." Do you mean language linguistically or in terms of style?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. I'd like to know exactly what it was they asked you to report on that led to you writing this particular report. You said you were asked to write about "this event." So how did they put the request to you? What were the terms of the request that led to you writing this particular report for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They read out to me a part of the book that relates to the alleged events in Qerim. I know where Qerim is located. It is located right next to the place that I'm talking about now where my soldiers were killed, Ljug Bunar, and on that occasion I described the events that I was familiar with, and I described whatever I knew to be true, namely that I remember very well the incident in which my soldiers got killed, that -- I said that I was in the immediate vicinity and that I have no knowledge whatsoever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Can I ask you now whether that was before or after you had read the parts of the book you say you read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, what do you mean "before or after"? I didn't understand. Did I write my statement before or after reading the statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My first -- my first question was about the terms in which the commission directed their question to you, and you answered that by saying they read out a part of the book to you. What I want to know now is whether that happened before or after you had read the book, as you say you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, they invited me. At that time I hadn't known about the book at all. They called me and they said, "Look, General, this book was published. It mentions certain things that allegedly happened in Djakovica. Please write whatever you know about the relevant events," and I wrote about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My question is a simple question. You say you had the book in your house for two days at one time. My question is: Was that before or after you were asked to write this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After I was asked to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, just give me one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you like to go, please, to tab 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you're not taking the point up, then, can I -- no, I want to complete it, in that case. My final question, then, General, is this: Did you write the report before or after you read the book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After I read the book -- rather, the part of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go to tab 29, please. Well, now, it's still your position, is it, that you had no documents to refer to, that you were asked to write reports, then shown the book, then wrote your report, so that we've got the information in hand. On this document -- have you got it there, tab 29? If Mr. Nort would be so good as to place the English version on the overhead projector. That's fine. That's fine. And you set out the preamble, and you say this: "Within the framework of the operation by the VJ and the MUP forces to neutralise the activities of the STS in the Trava sector, the unit participated in a seal-off operation on the following line: To the left, trig point 442; to the right trig 478 Batraki, aimed at preventing the withdrawal of the STS on the axis of Racaj village-Skivjan village." Do that from memory, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is based on the memory of the battalion commander who commanded that unit, Colonel Odak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that why your statement is so similar to his? We see his at tab 30.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think if everybody tells the truth about one event, then their accounts are very similar if not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now, look: You didn't get original materials, you haven't told us of anybody else asking for or being provided with original materials, but did Mr. Odak have original materials in order to give trig point references? Did he?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Odak took a map of Meja, because he's an infantryman, he knows what the deployment was, and he wrote those coordinates. I wrote that I toured those positions during the day and I found them there. When they were at their positions, I toured them, visited them during the day, just like I did with every other unit of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... maybe we are but I still want to get the method of writing the statement. Are you now saying you prepared your statement sitting there with Odak, or did he prepare a statement you believe from a map and show you the statement, or did he discuss it with you, or what? Because you can see the difficulty: Without a contemporaneous document, you couldn't be giving the trig point references and I want to know how you did it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote my statement based on the statement he wrote prior to that. Just as the commission gave me an assignment to write a statement, I gave him an assignment, as a subordinate officer who was on the spot at the relevant time, to write his own report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid there is some sort of confusion here, maybe because it was said in the same sentence, but the witness actually said that he had toured that unit on the ground. He didn't go to visit Odak while he was writing the statement. He said he toured the unit on the ground at the time when the unit was on the ground during that operation. That is the sense, the substance of what the witness said in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How does that help you with the position of the trig points? You've already told us you made your statement on the basis of Odak's statement.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Odak wrote a statement to me. I had been on that spot. Then I saw him there, and I confirmed that it was exactly as Mr. Odak has written. I confirmed that it's true, because I was there on the spot, on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Show me where your statement says, "I confirm the accuracy of Mr. Odak's statement," or would I be fair in suggesting that your statement reads as if it's your own recollection, reinforced however necessarily by contemporaneous documents or via some other means? Show us, where in the statement does it say, "I'm confirming what Odak says." It doesn't, does it? Have you ever as a senior officer disciplined any of your men? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you asked me two questions at the same time. Your first question was did I have to write that in my statement to the commission. If I should have written that, that's a different matter. I was satisfied that Odak wrote a truthful, accurate statement, and based on that, I wrote mine. If you think I should have added a clause that I am confirming his statement, that's something else. And the second question: Of course I took certain steps to punish my subordinates whenever they failed to comply with orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come back to that second question in just one more question. I'm grateful for your answering the first one in the way you did because it stimulates this question: So far as you know, was your practice of simply adopting someone else's statement as your own because you trusted him something that was standard for the commission?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you don't seem to be listening to me at all. I told you I was on the ground and I saw it with my own eyes. If I don't believe my own eyes, then who am I supposed to believe? I completely believe Lieutenant Colonel Odak's statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Don't divert attention by commenting on my question. Be so good as to go back to what you said. "I was satisfied that Odak wrote a truthful, accurate statement, and based on that, I wrote mine." Those are your words. Now, please tell the Court who is being -- please tell the Court who is -- which is being asked to take statements from people from the commission, was your practice of relying on somebody else's statement and then setting out the same yourself standard for the work done for the commission? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer with a yes or no, but I can tell you this: My practice was the following: Odak wrote a statement to submit to me, and I had no reason to doubt it. The same goes for other statements, such as the one by Colonel Vukasinovic. I know. I checked. I know exactly how it was. I didn't take --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- any statement at face value.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you turn to to check anybody's statements since you didn't have, so you tell us, the archives to hand? What did you go to to check?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you understand me when I'm saying that I was in the same place at the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- just as Odak was? I was there with my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please listen to the questions because we're listening to your answers. Your answer as translated was this: You dealt with the Odak statement, which you had no reason to doubt. You then said - and it may have been a slip by you - you said: "The same goes for other statements, such as the one by Colonel Vukasinovic. I know. I checked. I know exactly how it was."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: About some other event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, how did you check it? You either have a memory for something, in which case you don't need to read anybody else's statement, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or you read somebody else's statement and you go to some raw material and you say, "Aha, he's got it right; he says it was 10.30, the records show it was 10.30." What did you mean by saying you checked?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My subordinate officer wrote his statement, and when he wrote it he also consulted his subordinate officers in addition to his own memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I have no doubt to doubt -- no reason to doubt the statement of Lieutenant Colonel Odak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Therefore we have a pyramid of historians, do we? Subordinates reporting, making statements, and eventually it comes to you and you simply sign off it and say, "Yes, it's accurate," without us ever knowing whose actual memory is it. Would that be about right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, look at your statement, please, tab 29 once more, the second to last paragraph, where it says the seal-off operation on the said line was discontinued. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have the answer, the witness's answer on the transcript. He said, "Not correct." It's not correct, and we have no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He did indeed say that. It's not on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We now have that on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now look at the second to last paragraph. The seal-off operation on the said line was discontinued at 1600 hours. If we go to tab 30 in Odak, we see the references to the trig points, 442, 478, but nothing for the 28th. Who else should we look to to find this reference to 1600 hours, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose statement? We can look at the statement of somebody from the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did you write down and sign and seek to have presented to this Court as evidence something that says, "The seal-off operation was discontinued at 1600 hours"? What's your source of information for this bit?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a report of the duty officer who reported that the blockade is over.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where do we find that report?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have to ask for some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Don't you follow the point yet, Mr. Djosan? If you'd have to ask for some documents today, what did you do when you prepared this statement on the 27th of December, 2002? Did you ask for some documents? Did you have some documents? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you again: I called the Lieutenant Colonel Odak. He stated to me that at the time he had been at the relevant place, and I visited him at the time. I saw the deployment of my unit. I saw where they were, and it was sufficient to me to believe that it was so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not an answer to the question you've been asked. You're not doing yourself any justice in answering questions like this in the way you're answering them. You've said that the source of the information about the event at 1600 hours was a report from the duty officer, not from Colonel Odak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Lieutenant Colonel Odak did not write that. At least, I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the point that's being explored. You're being asked how you were able to make a statement to that effect without having any access to records and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, I didn't have any documentation at my disposal. I called Lieutenant Colonel Odak, and he wrote this statement for me, and that was enough for me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the problem with that, you see, the Prosecutor's pointing out to you, is there's no reference to this in Colonel Odak's statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think actually his last answer makes it clear that Odak actually wrote this statement for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's matter you can explore if you wish. I'm just directing attention to the point that you're making, I think, that Colonel Odak doesn't make any reference to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you answer His Honour's point, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that Lieutenant Colonel Odak did not write that may be just an omission. I cannot explain it right now. I can't explain why he didn't mention it in his statement. In fact, he is here, by the way, so you can ask him today or tomorrow. I cannot really account for this. Here's what Odak says, Lieutenant Colonel Odak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That answers my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And just because of your answers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I want to say something now, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered my question. If either counsel or Mr. Milosevic want to explore it further, that's a matter for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Djosan, in the course of dealing with His Honour's concerns, you said, "I called Lieutenant Colonel Odak, and he wrote this statement for me." Now, did you mean that, that in fact your statement, our tab 29, was actually written by Colonel Odak? You said.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. Just like the commission ordered me, I ordered him. Let me explain. Look, in Odak's statement, paragraph 2, he says: "Around 1600 hours I received an assignment to apply measures of combat security to return the unit into the composition of the battalion."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please put this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there's the statement of Colonel Odak. "Around 1600 hours, I received the assignment --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Djosan, the interpreter is asking to have it placed on the ELMO if you're going to be reading from it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I will. In the heading it says: "Lieutenant Colonel Vlatko Odak. Activities of the unit on the 28th of April, 1999. Statement. To the Commission for Cooperation with ICTY."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I haven't found the tab yet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's tab 30.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, not for us, I'm afraid. We'll have to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It seems to be the last page of 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Last page of 30.1 in the English, Mr. Nort, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I begin? "Around 1600 hours, I received the assignment to return the unit into the battalion while applying measures of combat security. Throughout this action, there was no activity by my unit or any other contact with the civilian population."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So there's no translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've got a translation. Yes, I've got a translation. There are three pages. I missed the third page on first looking at it. Mr. Nort, have you found it? There's a third page in English and it begins -- it's dated the 10th of January, 2002. So similar heading, but it's actually one page and it starts, "On the 28th of April, 1999." Have you got that in English? If not, I'll make mine available. There's one coming your way from the pro se liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you put the document that we saw just now again. Yes. I think there's a similar phrase in 30 and 30.1, in both of the documents. Is that one that we saw just now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's what we saw just now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's 30.1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you put the English version on, please, Mr. Nort. We've got the -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think it's an untranslated document within 30 rather than being in 30.1, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That's the point I raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a different sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I have in 30.1 a statement: "At around 1600 hours MUP units completed the terrain search and I was given the task of returning the unit to the battalion's defence sector." Is that not the same sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nort, could you put the last page in B/C/S in tab 30. I think that's the tab we saw just before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The page that comes from 30.1 in English, a single page, should be associated with a document we hitherto thought to be untranslated in tab 30, and in each case it begins with "On the 28th of April, 1999 ..." and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have it. I have it. But this is what the witness read out, a different one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's different again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Judge Kwon is holding the very document that I believe was the one the witness referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, if you could tell us whether this is the document you read out just now: "Around 1600 hours ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read the sentence again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "At around 1600 hours, I received the assignment with applying measures of combat security to take back the unit to within the composition of the battalion."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And that document wasn't translated. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please bear in mind -- yes, it's on now. Would you please bear in mind that in this tab 30 you will find two statements by Lieutenant Colonel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the name of the colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- on the 26th. One relates to the operations of the unit from the 20th to the 28th of April. That is the longer one which has been translated. And the second one, which is like a third page but it's a separate statement in fact of what the unit did on the 28th of April, 1999, and that is the one that he quoted just now. So had those two statements been given two tab numbers, there would be no misunderstanding. It's not the third page of the first statement, it's a separate statement which refers to the 28th of April, 1999, and which was quoted by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've now tracked down there is a statement, not yet translated, by Odak dealing in different terms with what happened at 1600 hours, and are you simply saying that you copied what Odak had said in his statement into your statement? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not related in a different way. It says that he, on the basis of my order, withdrew the unit from the line. So where is that different if you compare it to my assertion that everything was over at 1600 hours?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's second microphone be switched on, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I move back to one of the topics you've stimulated me to ask you about, which is the covering of Djakovica in "As Seen, As Told," can I seek your comment on the following: You left Djakovica, of course, in, what, June of 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No doubt you obtained some information on what happened in Djakovica afterwards, and I'd like your comment, if you can, on just the following three sentences: "The UCK/KLA, took control of the streets within hours of the Yugoslav and Serbian security forces' withdrawal from the municipality of Djakovica. It directed and assisted returning refugees to their homes and villages and quickly assumed policing duties, including traffic control. With this increasingly visible UCK presence came a rise in the number of allegations by victims and eyewitnesses in the municipality of UCK involvement in killings, abductions, detention, evictions, house burnings, harassment, and intimidation. There were numerous allegations of UCK involvement in attacks against minorities and Kosovo Albanians not deemed to be loyal to the UCK cause." Now, I know you'd left the area and would be subject -- would have available to you only hearsay information, but does that account of what the UCK did following the withdrawal of Serb troops seem to you to be about right? They took over what they could, and there was a rise in allegations of killings, abductions, detentions, evictions, burning, harassment, and intimidation by the KLA. Does that seem to you to be about right? And this relates to Djakovica specifically.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The KLA didn't do those things?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I would like -- no, that's not what I said. That's not the correct description of the event. My unit was the first to withdraw from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija because it was an air defence unit. Part of my unit remained in Djakovica, and that was the logistics battalion, for example, the forward command post of the Pristina Corps. And the KLA did not direct traffic. It was with the arrival of KFOR, with the arrival of KFOR that they began to reinforce their presence on the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What about the other bit, the bit about the KLA doing terribly bad things; killing, abducting, detaining, evicting, burning, harassing, and intimidating? Does that seem to you to be about right for what the KLA did at the arrival of KFOR and --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the arrival of KFOR, quite certainly. But before that, in the extent to which this was possible, they could have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware that allegations of that kind about the suffering of people at the hands of the KLA was obtained in another volume of a book "As Seen, As Told" prepared by the same organisation? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a lesser extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did anybody bother to provide you with this book as a balanced view of events in Kosovo over all? Did anybody show you this book, "As Seen, As Told, Part II"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That book cannot offer a balanced view of the position -- about the position that prevailed in Kosovo and Metohija. I was the head of the commission for the application of a Military Technical Agreement, and I had knowledge on that basis --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... time. Could you answer the question: Did anybody show you this book?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen that book, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it has --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, let's go to the book that you say you were shown and that you say you read. If we could have the version on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The part which relates to Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed so. Not all of it. It would take far too long. But if Mr. Nort -- I'm afraid it's in English -- if we could go to page 170. And because we don't have the English -- the Serb version here, because you haven't got the page references or chapter references or whatever, all I can do is explain to you the format of the bit on Djakovica. There is a historical passage, which you can see. That's a reference to the Jakupi family. Do you remember the Jakupi family? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can see here are names and figures. That's as far as I can follow English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No complaints about that. I'm just trying to give you the structure of the book in English because you tell us you've seen the same book but -- which will therefore have the same structure, but in Serbian. So a historical section, a passage about the Jakupi family, then a bit about Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next page, please. In fact, if we could try to have the whole book in view for the time being. If you could come out of focus a bit. That's excellent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then there's a passage about Djakovica town, and we can see events before the 20th of March. That's dealt with. Next page, please, Mr. Nort. And then it goes over the page and we see it turns to events after the 20th of March of 1999. That's down towards the bottom. And if we can go to the right-hand side and focus on the column that's currently at the right-hand side of the screen, it says this as one observation. I'll read you this passage: "The beginning of NATO airstrikes against the FRY on the 24th of March triggered an immediate intensification of the violence and destruction in the centre of Djakovica, in the course of which many houses were burned, shops looted and Kosovo Albanian citizens killed." Now, tell us, please, thinking back, and your memory is good enough to cover two and a half years from -- three and a half years from events to making a statement, so do your best: Did you read this sentence in the version that came to you? The sentence that suggested an immediate intensification of violence and destruction.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, this isn't clear to me here, but let me -- if I believe the interpretation I've received, or the translation, then possibly that's what was written, but that's not how it was. That is not how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... we'll come to how it was in a second. Now, you're a literate man. Just look down, please, at the text a little bit more closely, and Mr. Nort will point his finger to where we see "Albanian citizens killed." Put your finger there, please, Mr. Nort. Three lines down from the top. Now, you see where Mr. Nort's finger is, you see something called a footnote. If Mr. Nort would be good enough, please, now temporarily, keeping his finger in page 173 to go on to page 187. 187, please, right-hand side. Thank you. Right-hand side. Is that 187? It can't be. Page 187. Yes. Back a bit. There we go. Right. Now, you see on the right-hand side here we've got footnote 23, and it sets it all out there and identifies by pseudonyms one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 different witnesses. Did you at any stage discover that allegations made about what happened in Djakovica were said by "As Seen, As Told" to be based on, for example, this bit, 15 different witnesses? Did you discover that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, how would I be able to establish or discover the statements of 15 witnesses under pseudonyms when I know the witness whose commander I was? I know him personally. I know his name and his surname, and I know that he wasn't telling the truth. Now, you're expecting me to look for 15 pseudonyms and to see whether they were telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that. In fact, if you interpret it in that way, it's my error, of course.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me just make it clear to you. You're in a court of law where evidence is being presented to the Judges. What we're concerned -- I'm concerned to discover the system whereby the evidence presented through you is coming. That's why I want to know what you actually did before preparing the statements that you say you prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness had earlier said when he was shown the passage from the book that that is not how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And I wanted to hear his version of how it happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Upon the departure of my unit from Djakovica, and that was on the 11th of June, 1999, in the early hours of the morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How it was relates to a quotation from the book but the witness is unable to follow the quotation from the book which he doesn't have. And the quotation from the book related to the assertion marked by Mr. Nice in the footnote, according to which on the 24th of March, that is to say the first day of the aggression or, rather, with the aggression, the killing of Albanians and setting fire to houses in the centre of Djakovica started. And he said a moment ago, and he assumed that it was correctly translated, but that that was not how it was, and the witness is now saying what happened when he left after the war. So you must establish this link between what the witness is being asked. A moment ago he was quoted about the 24th of March, how the killing of Albanians started and the burning of houses in the centre of Djakovica. That was the quotation read out to him from the book and then the footnote about the 15 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was actually referring to the passage which ended with the killing of Albanian citizens, and the witness interrupted and said that's not how it happened, and I thought he should be allowed to say how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Would Your Honour like to take the witness to it or would you like me to deal with it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think you should do that, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To clarify matters, Mr. Djosan, the book alleges that on the 20 -- or triggered by events on the 24th of March there was an intensification of violence and destruction in the course of which many houses were burned, shops were looted, and Kosovo Albanian citizens were killed. When that was read out to you and before I turned you to the question I wanted you to answer about system, you volunteered this was not how it happened. His Honour would like you to explain that answer, and in particular, I think, he would like you to explain how things on or immediately after the 24th of March happened have come to be reflected in this book as a description increasing violence, looting, and killing.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the 24th of March, and I said that the first bombs and the first night a bomb fell on Djakovica, and that it also fell on our barracks, which was located in Djakovica and that I was at Cabrat at the time, that soon after that I saw flames in Katolicka Street, and that after that, in the following days, I was witness to daily operations by the NATO Air Force and their targeting Djakovica and the surrounding parts. Under conditions of that kind, there were all kinds of things happening, and the Siptar terrorists launched their operations to coincide with the first NATO bombs that fell. Once the NATO aggression had been unleashed, at the same time all the Siptar terrorists, for which I said had been hiding in the houses as well and were not able or dared leave them, suddenly they activated themselves, and simultaneously there was shooting in town. And I described that in my book as well. But that's not important, that's not the important point. What is important is that that is what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... your account, every word of this last sentence - if Mr. Nort could take us back to page 173, please, left-hand column, middle of the page - every word of this account is false. No looting, no killing, no burning at all. Hmm?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right, not correct. There was burning, I said. I saw from Cabrat Katolicka Street burning, and if a whole street is burning, then there is burning. I'm not saying that there wasn't any looting. After the bomb fell, windows shattered on shop windows, the glass shattered, and of course it was normal that there was looting too, that this was accompanied by looting. So I didn't say there was no looting and no burning; yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's read on the next sentence, please. Or just the end of the paragraph, and I'll read slowly. Please follow me: "During the night, police officers and paramilitaries set the old market quarter on fire. Some of the paramilitaries present were described as wearing camouflage uniforms with a tiger's face on the sleeve patches. Local residents also identified local Serbs and 'Gypsies' (Maxhupet) as participating and shooting directly into houses of Kosovo Albanian residents." And then this last sentence: "Tanks, trucks and heavy artillery were seen in the town." So the allegation is quite specific as to who were the seen, visible wrongdoers, the police and paramilitaries, and that the highest that the army gets as a reference at this stage is of tanks being seen in the town. Is this not indeed an accurate account?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not an accurate account at all, and it's very specific, and with the specifics, you're quite right. First of all, I said there were no paramilitary formations. That's the first point. Secondly, what tanks in town? And what tanks at all once the bombardment had started? A tank wouldn't have survived even five minutes if above it there were so many hostile planes flying. It would only have been a mad commander who would have led his tanks into town. Our tanks were all entrenched, camouflaged, and they were not operative. Any operation on the part of the tank would mean its immediate destruction. So that statement is a specific one, you're right there, but I don't want to use another worse term how I would term it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, do you remember yesterday -- not yesterday, last week when we were looking at the statements of -- yes, Captain Peraj, Mr. Peraj, he was quite distinct about your good qualities and your limited involvement in these offences, and I suggested to you that that was a reflection of his being an honest account. Where we look at a compilation from a large number of sources, we are going to see that the army might be shown in Djakovica in a different role from the police and paramilitaries. I'm going make the same suggestion to you, that it's actually a fair and balanced account. Now, we've got a Serb version now, at least I think of this part of events, and so I can take you to the next reference to the army, and so far we've just seen tanks, then the next one, I think -- yes. If you'd be good enough to look -- Mr. Nort, if you could come and just hand the -- this document to the witness, where my thumb is there, the join of two paragraphs. And then just follow it from about there, and Mr. Nort will take us to the right-hand side of this page. Further up. Further up, please. Bring the book down. That's the stuff. Thank you. You see this entry at the end of one paragraph, we see these sentences, speaking of people who fled "for fear of being expelled by Yugoslav or Serbian forces, they went to relatives or friends in other parts of the town or to villages in the nearby hills so that about half the population remained in the town at the end of the NATO bombing, according to local estimates, as compared with other towns, including Pec in particular, which were virtually empty." Is it right, as recorded here, it was only about half of the population that fled or went into hiding?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me answer the first part of your question. There were no paramilitaries in the town of Djakovica or in Kosovo and Metohija either. The second point, in Djakovica --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to bring you back to this. I'm afraid I'm going to take more time than I wanted. Do you remember last week you made broad allegations -- not allegations, assertions, and before I asked you questions, the learned Judges tested you from time to time and said, "Well, are you saying that? Did you mean to say that?" I'm going to ask you the same thing before we move on. Are you saying that there were no paramilitaries anywhere in Kosovo? Take your time before answering because if you -- because I want to test you if you're going to say that there were no paramilitaries anywhere in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state that in Kosovo and Metohija there were no paramilitary formations on the basis of knowledge received by briefing and reports from corps commanders. As for Djakovica, I know that even more directly and we had briefings and reporting in the corps command. We had information coming in from the corps command, and never ever did I hear any piece of information indicating that that there were paramilitaries anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go back, then, to the people fleeing from the hills and half the population remaining. Is that right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To what extent that is true, whether it was half or more or less, I don't know. But how do you explain that they started to flee the same day the planes started to fly? It's like they agreed. How come there wasn't fear before? Why didn't they start fleeing ten days earlier or a month earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at the end of the following paragraph, just to see the accuracy of this book. Where it says -- after dealing with other things, it says: "An interviewee saw the VJ moving from their barracks into a compound at the San Antonio Catholic church." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: St. Anthony church was almost in the barracks. It was a stone's throw away. A soldier could have jumped --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- from the barracks into the church --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- if you know where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then finally, if the Court will indulge me, if we go over to page 174. One example of the way the things are associated with paramilitaries but not with the military, if we look at the bottom of page 170 -- right at the bottom of page 174. Right at the bottom. Put it up further, please. Further, further. Right up. Keep going. That's it. The sentence there on the left-hand side: "On that day and following --" that which was the 28th of March, and on following days, -- "police continued to go from house to house, street to street in Djakovica --" top of the next column, please, Mr. Nort -- "telling people to leave (often using loudspeakers) and ordering people to go to Albania. One refugee's report of rumours that Serbian forces took women to the Djakovica football stadium and sexually abused them there had not at the time of the writing been substantiated. However, several interviewees reported that young women were abducted by Serbian police and paramilitaries." You see, the way this book is written, so far as Djakovica is concerned, is with a focus on police and paramilitaries, and I want to know what it is you say you were shown that led to you making the denial in your statement that you did. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, that's very simple. I was in Djakovica. I was commander of the garrison. I've never seen any paramilitary units. I am not aware nor have I ever heard at briefings, whereas I should have as garrison commander, anything like that. My subordinate officers were all over town. They should have told me if they had seen anything of the kind. Nik Peraj should have told me. He was the one who should have told me if that had been the case. Not only him, everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... at these. I don't know if the Court had any intention of rising --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think we --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is now a passage in Serb of the relevant -- It's the passage on Djakovica, and if the witness wishes not to rest but to use Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the time in the interval looking at that passage, it's a matter for him, but we're happy for him to take the document with him to his room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. You may take the document. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Djosan, I don't know if you took the opportunity to review the Serb version of "As Seen, As Told," and I make no complaint if you didn't. Just tell me, are you able now to identify any passage in that book that you read and to which you responded in your statement, our tab 7, saying: "I have read the information that the 'forces of the FRY allegedly took part in the destruction of those parts of the town,'" meaning Djakovica. Have you been able to identify that passage in the text you've been provided?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have availed myself of the opportunity to check during the break, and I found the same style, the same authors, the same way of writing, and I can find countless examples of obvious untruths. And I am just looking at one passage like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then you better tell us which passage it is. First of all, tell us the heading because the page numbers won't assist us. Tell us the heading and we'll get it placed on the overhead projector by Mr. Nort. What's the heading?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Meja, including the first bombing of the convoy of displace the persons."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 178, possibly 179. Is it the first, second, third or fourth paragraph of that passage?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The right column, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... organised. Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you call this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be -- yes. It will be on page 179, Mr. Nort, and it will be towards the top of the page, on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please read the passage you say is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it talks about Meja, including the first bombing of a convoy of displaced persons by NATO. "According to a statement of a 13-year-old boy --" in fact, another statement by a 13-year-old boy -- "displaced from Pacaj (near Dobros, Djakovica) that morning, described how as he reached Meja he heard an explosion as a tractor was hit. The police ordered a group into a large three-storey building and a garage. The boy said that after about 15 minutes they were bombed for about 20 minutes by camouflaged military planes, after which he, his mother, and about 40 others ran from the village to the mountains, where they met UCK/KLA forces who advised them to go in the direction of Ramoc. The UCK then became involved in fighting with the police, and after about an hour the villagers were called by the police to 'come and see their dead relatives.' He said that in the bombing of the house, about seven people were killed, including the boy's two sisters and two other members of his family, while he and his mother were also wounded. He also said that many others were killed 'as a result of the shelling of the tractor.' (See further Chapter 13, human shields and other endangerment of non-combatants during military operations.)"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you say is wrong about that and why?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everything is wrong. Jamie Shea spent so much time explaining how those planes flew and how they came to hit that column. One of these accounts must be wrong. I was near the place. Two F-16 planes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question is what's wrong with the account that's been read out to you or that you're -- sorry, that you're reading from. What's wrong with that? Where has that account --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this whole account is wrong, especially the part where he says that the police followed them and that from that place they went to the forest to fight with the KLA. Does that sound logical to you? And if this book is based on accounts by 13-year-old boys, then I'm not surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you there where this 13-year-old boy says he was? Yes or no. Were you physically there yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived after the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... actually at this place near Dobros where the tractor was hit?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tractor, yes, I was there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How soon were you there after the tractor was hit?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about half an hour, maybe an hour later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you can't say what the police did, can you? You see, this book isn't actually complaining about the army at this stage. It's complaining about the police. So this is your best -- your first example, probably your best example, of why the book is unreliable. You weren't even there, Mr. Djosan, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had been there, I would have been killed too. If I had been there at that moment. But I arrived half an hour later, half an hour after the NATO planes bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't have time to go into it any more. Is there any other example from the passage you've read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just ask the witness whether he received any reports that would have contradicted the version in the section that we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't receive any special report that would contest that, but I contest it based on my visit there, my statement, and the knowledge I gained on the ground. If police had been there, at least one policeman would have been killed too. They can't have been so lucky as not to have lost a single man if they had been there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You just said -- made reference to the knowledge that you gained on the ground. That's what I had in mind, whether you were told anything when you arrived there that would contradict what we just read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I talked to the man who was at the head of the column. I tried to explain that, but I was interrupted. When I came to the spot, I talked personally with a man who was leading the column. It was a man, an older man. He told me that they were walking. He didn't mention the police at all. He spoke about two planes, and he pointed his finger in the direction where they left, and that direction coincides with the direction indicated to me by my soldiers who were observing the airspace. He didn't say a single word about four planes or camouflage colour of the planes or the police. All he told me he told me in excellent Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I understand the Prosecutor to be asking about is where in this book you saw reference to allegations about the army. Now, the passage you've referred to doesn't make any complaint about the army. And unless I'm misunderstanding this, it seems you haven't been able to identify a part where there's a complaint about the army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not correct. What I'm trying to say is I didn't come here to defend the army. I came here to tell the truth based on the knowledge I have. I never covered up any crimes whenever I learnt about any. You can see that from the criminal reports that I filed against my own soldiers in cases of attempted rape. So it is not my intention here to defend the army. That's not my capacity in which I'm appearing here. I came to speak about the knowledge I gained in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... His Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Djosan, it relates to the statement you made on the -- well, about the events of the 24th of March, but it's tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 28th of November, 2002, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where you say: "I have read the information that the forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia allegedly took part in the destruction of those parts of the town in a book published by the Humanitarian Law Centre." Now, what we're trying to find are the passages in the book that you read that said the army took part in the destruction of parts of Djakovica. And you say you've looked through the book and you found such passage but we haven't identified any yet. Now, is there a passage there that you've been able to find that says that? It's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
