utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a simple question, I agree, but it's difficult to find such a passage in a book like this. It would take me time. In a book like this where every passage speaks about destruction, some paramilitary units, crimes, it's simply impossible to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Djosan, I must deal with matters as summarily as I can. The short truth is this, isn't it: The VJ commission was not just -- it was not in any sense there for cooperation. It was there to filter out adverse material, or adverse to the VJ, the police, and the -- or the VJ in particular, and to enable people like you to provide statements that would whitewash the activities of the VJ in particular in the course of this conflict. That's what it was doing, and you responded to that because you're a weak man, as Captain Peraj said you were.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by a weak man, but let's set that aside. What you said about the commission is not true. What about Nik Peraj says about me? One day he compliments me, another day he says I'm a weak man. In fact, I understand that Nik Peraj wrote two statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go back to an earlier question of mine and then I must move on. In disciplining soldiers within your command, did you have things like court -- courts-martial? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did courts-martial take evidence not only -- I'm sorry. Did courts-martial in your system allow accused soldiers or subordinate officers to give evidence on their own behalf? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I did not interfere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not interfere with the decision of the court, just as I ignore the way this Court works.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ever sit on a court-martial as an adjudicator?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the accused in those circumstances allowed to give evidence to defend himself?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the person who was asked to give a statement, and if you call that giving evidence, I gave a statement. I don't know what you mean by that notion giving evidence. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- believe that I'm testifying now here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm trying to get an answer from you, Mr. Djosan, although I think it's absolutely obvious. If you were on a court-martial trying someone, would you expect to hear from witnesses giving their own accounts of evidence or would you expect to hear witnesses retelling accounts given to them by other people who were also available to give evidence? Which would you expect?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never sat in on a court-martial. I gave a statement before an investigating judge. I have never been part --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of a court chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I was never in a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The VJ commission, in doing all the things it did, was trying to corrupt history.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we go into private session for one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may come back to that, but I doubt I'll have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's revert, please, to Meja. The summary position is that allegations are to the effect that there was an ethnic cleansing operation in revenge for the killing of a policeman, and to that you say not at all, this was a terrorist-only combat. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the KLA at that stage was a very formidable enterprise, was it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time and at any other time, it was a paramilitary terrorist organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... wasn't it? A pretty frightening group of people.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a paramilitary organisation, a terrorist one, with very large number of members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed we can find this, although I'm not going to take the time to do so, we can find Ojdanic in a Supreme Defence Council meeting, Exhibit 667, tab 73, held on the 25th of December, 1998, saying that certainly in respect of the border areas 90 per cent of the inhabitants had a negative attitude towards the security services. By implication, a very large majority of people supported the KLA at that time. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know what Ojdanic said. Ojdanic is five rungs higher on the ladder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... people probably supported the KLA and 90 per cent of the people were hostile to the VJ forces, to the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were not so many people among the civilian population who supported the terrorist KLA organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, armed, dangerous, and frightening. Would you accept that for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would rather say that they were a terrorist organisation on a territory of a sovereign state. A paramilitary terrorist organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look, if we may, at the way -- at the way Mr. Peraj drew the operation, just so that we can remind -- here it comes. It's part of Exhibit 143. I didn't give Ms. Dicklich warning and I want to save time. This is the way Mr. Peraj drew this, with the army in support formation, enabling the MUP to drive down innocent Kosovo Albanians to Meja, where it killed them. Thank you. That's the way it's been put against the general forces of Serbia. I'd like to you tell me, please, how many casualties were suffered by the army or the police in the course of these two days fighting against, as you would say, this formidable - or however you describe it - terrorist force? How many?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit did not suffer a single casualty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Fine. Next unit --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nor was there any wounding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next unit, please. You know all about everything that happened. How many casualties, please? How many casualties?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Might --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And why would I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Might it -- Mr. Djosan, you have been telling this Court of your knowledge of all sorts of matters outside your immediate area of responsibility. Are you really telling us that in as significant and notorious an event as the Meja conflict, if it was a conflict, you're unaware as to whether any of your brother soldiers or fellow police officers, in the degree to which they would be fellows, suffered? I just want know. There may have been some. I want you to take me to the material that would show how many.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely that. I don't know because my unit that took part had no casualties. The others who took part were not subordinate to me nor were they my superiors, so they weren't duty-bound to inform me, nor did they have the need to inform me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us, if the VJ and MUP forces suffered no casualties, might it just have been a matter of good luck? Do you remember using the word good luck earlier when you described how people present at the scene of a bombing would be lucky to escape? Was it again just good luck that there were no victims on the Serb side, if there were no victims on the Serb side in this two-day period?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I did not say that there were no losses in the other units of the army of Yugoslavia or the MUP. What I was talking about was my own unit. So there's no room for good luck here. I didn't mention good luck. And as far as good luck is concerned, I put it into context and said that not every bomb kills, not every bullet in wartime kills. Because if every bomb killed, then no people would have survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Djosan, you know, of course, about Racak, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard about it. I heard about it. Yes, there's been talk about Racak recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, in Racak there were no Serb-side victims. Somebody apparently suffered an injury that would have been worse but for deflection of the bullet from some source. Help us, please: Are these reflections of the same thing, revenge attacks with an absolute excess of force determined to kill whatever men it was wanted to kill?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't want -- know what you mean by "revenge." Racak was completely outside my area of responsibility, so I don't know about any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's review, then, a little bit about your own body, I think, at the material time with the extracts from the war diary now provided, we are told, insofar as they were available to the accused. But as they're being distributed, and don't look to them yet, Mr. Djosan, you can listen to this question and we can save time, did your forces, that is the VJ forces, deploy an intervention platoon in this operation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was an intervention platoon, first of all? What was its nature?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that during that period of time in the town of Djakovica there were my non-combat men, portions of my unit, which means the command artillery battalion and the logistics battalion. At that point in time, the attacks had already started, attacks on members of our unit. And it was a platoon or, rather, a unit made up of soldiers who were duty-bound, in case of an attack on the unit, to be ready to intervene or, rather, to defend themselves, just as any unit has its separate unit to protect it. So that was that platoon, the platoon defending the command post of the brigade, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. So did the intervention platoon, if that was its proper function, have to do in the activity at or near Meja on the 27th and 28th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were given the assignment by our superior command, by the forward command post, that our unit, the one described, should set up a blockade at the portion we've already mentioned of the territory, at the features and elevations that were stipulated, with the aim of preventing any overflow of terrorists from the area of Meja or, rather, that was the Carragojs valley already, not to reach town, to enter town. And it was in town that our units were deployed, the logistics battalion, the command platoon, the rear troops, and they could have been jeopardised by operations that the terrorists engaged in. So any normal unit would have forces for its own defence or to defend the most important part of its deployment and men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The intervention force was just in some way defensive; is that right? It's called intervention but it's actually defensive; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely that. Yes, exclusively defensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you got with you, please, a copy of the Reka plan? Have you got with you a copy of the Reka plan?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, why would I have it here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know what it is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just confirm this: If a party such as the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal has been denied access to documents such as this by the commission or by the VJ itself, there's no way, is there, it could even know the name Reka plan, or Rijeka plan, as it's known in other sources? There is no way it could have known of the existence of that plan, is there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question? Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... yeah. This isn't a public plan. This wasn't published, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Public plan. Would you please ask me a concrete question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've made an observation, but give us a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us what the Reka plan was.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an assignment to prevent the grouping of Siptar terrorist forces which had been rallying forces in the Carragojs valley with the aim of strengthening and reinforcing the forces that at that time had come in from Kosare and were attacking with great force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was the plan, it would sound, that led to the things that happened on the 27th and 28th of April, 1999, and that led to a large number of deaths in the Meja region. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened in the Meja region, but I do know what the role of my unit was in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... please. You know what the Reka plan is because you've told us yes. The Reka plan is the --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- by which you and everyone else acted in the Meja region on the 27th and 28th of April. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. Function, act, what do you mean? To function has a different concept. Within the frameworks of that programme, I had my own assignment and task, and that's all I can tell you about that. I do know that the plan was called Reka. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it still exists. Unless it's been destroyed, there will be a copy of the plan somewhere, won't there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I don't have it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you think as a general, you tell us qualifying intellectually at the level of a Ph.D., that to know what happened in a war it would be helpful to know what the plan was? Do you think that might be helpful?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be extremely helpful to learn about everything that went on in the war. That would be highly useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Djosan, let me make it quite clear: My suggestion to you is that you're doing everything you can because you have no choice but to whitewash the VJ and that by your last answer you're making this absolutely clear. You're giving yourself away. I gave you a very simple question, now would you please answer it. I'm going to read it out to you in full.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, do that, please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you think that it would be helpful -- to know what happened in a war, do you think it would be helpful to know what the plan was? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be helpful for all the plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Djosan?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Do you accept that until we saw these papers produced this morning that had been available to the accused but that had not been translated or transcribed for us, that we had no knowledge, as far as I'm aware, of the name Reka plan as the plan that dealt with what happened at Meja on these two days in April 1999? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, can you think of any good reason why a body that describes itself as a commission seeking to cooperate with the Office of the Prosecutor and the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia should not voluntarily produce through a witness like you or someone else the very plan that led to the killings in Meja? Can you think of any good reason why that plan should not be produced?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "killings in Meja" I don't think is appropriate. But how do you know that the commission would not have done that had it not been abolished on the first day after the minister of the interior had been appointed? And I don't want to mention the way in which that was done. Perhaps the commission would have sent that in, would have provided it. Perhaps it wasn't given an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness misspoke and said the minister of foreign affairs, and in the transcript it says minister of the interior whereas the witness meant the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant to say the minister of defence, Mr. Borislav Tadic, who was minister of defence at that time. So had he not abolished it, quite certainly we would find it easier to discuss this matter here and now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, dealing with your earlier point, the commission had been effective and in operation for two years, so it had plenty of time to provide this material at the time that it was taking statements from you and Odak and Vukovic and all the others, so there is no problem there in providing the plan, is there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, how far it was operational or not. I know that I gave the statement to the commission. Now, how it functioned, I don't know. All I know is that I provided it with the statement, and you have the document to prove that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when Tadic abolished the commission, was it in an atmosphere where allegations were implied or made that the commission had been acting dishonourably or dishonestly? Was that the undercurrent of its abolition in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been brought up to enter into the minister's head and his ideas. He was the minister of the army. What he wanted, what he intended, it's not up to me to comment nor do I know about that, nor did he ask me whether to abolish it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we now look at the additional bundle of documents, which, of course, is as yet untranslated. And I can simply asked ask Mr. Nort to place the pages of a spare copy on the overhead projector, for the witness to have his own copy. They came from the accused. I haven't page numbered them, but if we work first of all from the back, Mr. Nort, and on the bundle that we've got come in about six pages, you'll come to a document that looks like this, a document that looks like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document shows, does it not, that the war diary of which a very limited number of pages has been provided, and initially less translated into English, actually contains 198 pages, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I inquired later on about this stamp here that contains this fact of 198. It is introduced when an empty diary, an notebook of a diary is handed -- issued to a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is not a proper comment. A question has been asked of the witness. Let the witness answer it. It's not for you to provide the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I provided an explanation last time, if you remember. I gave you an explanation, but I didn't know this piece Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of information so I've just added that to the explanation already given by me earlier on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to explain? Every command has a book of so-called recorded notebooks, books and so forth. When an empty notebook is issued, or book - let's say notebook - then pages are put on the notebook and you will find the numbers of the pages at the top, and at the end there is a clause which states that that notebook has so many pages, such-and-such number of pages, and it is certified, and here it was the clerk in the department, Captain Dobrivoj Vasic, who authenticated this. And then at the bottom it says it was registered and recorded in the control book of registered books of the military post of 1946, which is that military post, certified books. So the brigade that I was in command had a military post, and it was 1936. That was the number of the military post. Once you have a diary or notebook that has been completed, filled in, all the pages used up and is handed over, it must have the same number of pages. Not all the pages have to be filled in. And had the aggression lasted even longer, perhaps all the pages would have been filled in in that unhappy event. By that is the proceedings that are always followed with records, daily records, with a -- with a record of the targets. Every empty notebook, which is an official document, must be certified, and that means that this war diary has been recorded and registered by the control book of the certified books, and it is found on page 40 and its number is 552, and it says "War Diary," and that's where it says how many pages the diary has. That's what all this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And how many pages does it have?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As many days as there were war days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many pages does the diary have? That's all we want to know. Simple enough question.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say just off the top of my head. I don't have the war diary before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But sometimes in a war diary you would use up one page, sometimes two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But at any event, all the pages must be in their proper place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nort, if you would good enough now to go to the beginning and we'll try to work through it from the beginning because that's the only way to make sense out of it, and we'll deal with it page by page, starting at the beginning. Page 1, please. Or not the cover sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This covers the 24th of March, and I've got nothing to ask about. The next sheet covers a bit more of the same, I think. It takes us to the 25th. And then the next sheet after that goes a bit further. Now, the next sheet starts off on the 28th of March. Is it right that if we look at the entry for 21.15 we see the MUP -- sorry, the VJ reinforcing the MUP. Just read out 21.15, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. "One platoon of the above should reinforce the MUP in the Junik area. Ordered by the commander, the commander of the 3rd."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And does this reflect typical joint operations by the MUP and VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the MUP and the army of Yugoslavia from time to time in specific situations when there was the threat that members of the MUP would be in an adverse position, they would help each other out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was subordinated to whom?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody was subordinated to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. And then 21.16, read that one out, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another 3 BOVs, or combat armoured vehicles, should reinforce the MUP detachment in the Junik area, and this was ordered by the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps. I ordered the command of the artillery battalion, and I was ordered by the head of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps was? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an officer who was at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica, and he had the right, in the name of the commander, to issue orders to us other commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The commander at that time being?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So Lazarevic is able to order the VJ to act with the MUP, and it happened on a regular enough basis. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That happened when there was the danger of the terrorists killing or, rather, destroying members of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next page, please, Mr. Nort. Now, this goes down to and starts the entry for the 31st of March. We're now into the eighth day of the war, as it says on the right. Turn over the page, please, Mr. Nort, to pick up a point I was making earlier. There is some reference here to casualties, which is one of the things I've been looking for. Perhaps you'd like to read out the reference to the deaths, I think, of Djordje Cimbaljevic, and if you can find --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cimbaljevic, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- third line down, I think.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just read an account of the deaths, so that we've got that, and the wounded, Aleksandar Tadic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the radar that was hit and destroyed, the following people were killed and burnt, in brackets, soldiers Cimbaljevic Milic Djordje, born on the 17th of June, 1979 in Barani [phoen], Montenegro, in the army of Yugoslavia from the 23rd of September, 1998, and Ivanovic Tomislav, father's name Zoran, born on the 22nd of July in Trstenik, a Serb serving in the army of Yugoslavia from the 24th of June, 1998."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... these two, and I think Aleksandar Tadic, if that's the right chap, who was injured, injured in bombing. They're not injured or killed -- killed or injured in bombing, not by the KLA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Let's move on. Next page. We now see -- we come to the 1st of April. There's a different format, just in case we have to think about it, because we don't have the original. Can you explain the different format?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply because keeping a war diary is not prescribed especially. In a war diary what is entered is events which are important for a particular day, for a particular event that occurred that has to do with the unit. And another thing, war diaries were not always kept by the same people. An officer who happened to be at the headquarters in the staff kept the war diary. And they would have furlough, they would change shifts, so it wasn't always the first -- the same person that kept the war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know who kept this page, for example, the 1st of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No reason to doubt the --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No reason to doubt the reliability or the accuracy of what these people were writing down, is there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: None at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No reason whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... second page of what appears to be the 1st of April. Perhaps you'd read out the entry at 11.50, four lines down, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "The guards from Cabrat noticed a group of 30 Albanians pulling out of the town to Krunic -- Lieutenant Krunic was told to keep them, hold them back until the MUP had arrived. A large group of Albanians left the town. Between 1800 hours and 2100 hours, pursuant to orders from the brigade commander, there was a change of command post from the Kuca Maslenica point to the cultural centre at Djakovica. The conditions for life and work at this command post were favourable. On this day, NATO -- there was no NATO operations against our units nor our units -- nor did our units target NATO planes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... a lot of these documents and the printed orders of the army are careful to refer to all Kosovo Albanians, I must suggest, as terrorists, but on this occasion it slipped through. They're just described as Albanian men who were being kept back. Why? Why were you keeping Albanian men back in the middle of a war? No reference to them being terrorists, no reference to them being KLA, just Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Not all Albanians were terrorists, and not all Albanians were members of the KLA. Not all of them even supported the KLA. Had these people here been terrorists, then they would have shot at my soldiers. And Lieutenant Krunic would not have occasion -- would not have been able to keep them back, hold them back, 30 of them. And one platoon numbers 20 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... why shouldn't they be allowed to go free to determine their own destinies?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They passed through the deploy -- our unit's deployment and our unit was at Cabrat, deployed at Cabrat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidentally, before we move on and before I forget it, you made an observation earlier about the coincidence of people leaving the territory of Kosovo and Metohija at the start of the bombing. There's a very simple explanation for that, as you will well know, and that is that nobody really believed that this accused was actually going to walk away from the possibility of negotiation until the very last minute when it actually happened. Nobody believed he'd actually allow the bombing to happen, but he did and it was thus that people delayed - those who were going leave delayed - leaving until that moment. Isn't that the truth or part of the truth?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are your insinuations. First of all, Mr. Milosevic did not allow the bombing to start. Somebody else allowed it. And one day we will hear the truth loud and clear. Second, people started to flee on that day from Belgrade and other cities and towns as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You received some of those people in your cities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next page, please, just to make sure that the Court can be -- next page takes us to the 2nd of April. Next page to the 3rd of April, Mr. Nort. The following page to more of the 3rd of April. And then we have a change of format - next page, please - and we're now on the 7th of April. Next page, please. 8th of April. And then we come to the next page, which is the 25th of April. Now, we turn over from the 25th, we come to the, I think -- yes, the 27th. So I don't know what -- next page, please. I simply don't know where the 26th is. It hasn't been provided. Can you think of any reason why the page from the 26th ought to have been extracted from these papers? Anything happen on the 26th of which you're particularly embarrassed or ashamed, anything?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I'm not ashamed of anything, and as for that page missing, it's not the only page that's missing. If you get hold of the complete diary, you will see that every page is in its place and that it completely coincides with the transcribed version over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally have no reason to be ashamed of anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just remind us of what you said. This is your -- your group's war diary. You're principally concerned with air defence.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you read out, please, for us the first entry on the 27th of April and tell us what indications we have for timing. "Putarak" [phoen] is the word we have on the left-hand side, I think. What does that tell us, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says it was the 7th [sic] of April. That year it was a Tuesday. The entry goes like this: "With greater intensity that on the previous day, the enemy aviation is violating our airspace."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Read on.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "From the very morning --" Just a minute. I'm finding it hard to read this handwriting. "Its action is targeted on standard installations like Devet Jugovica barracks and the MUP facility. The clearing operation Reka involving --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness read a bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The forces that were involved."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Djosan, please read more slowly for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it will help the Court to know that we have just, I think, reached the line beside 0600, or possibly the line just above the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you pick it up again where you started with "The clearing operation Reka," and read that slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The action of clearing Siptar terrorist forces Reka has started. It involves a mixed battery of the 1st Self-propelled Platoon, one infantry platoon from the logistics battalion, and two infantry battalions. The action is going according to plan, as envisaged. Due to the absence of the commander, the Chief of Staff is leading the action Reka. Organs of the command started the work according to plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, we focus on that, but in order to save any anxiety of the Court as to how long this exercise will take, if you look down the rest of the page, and we'll come back to this entry, 0830, 11, 12, 15, 18, 19, are those all entries that relate to air defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is one wounded soldier referred to at 12 -- 1200 hours, I think. Is it a name Ilic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. Toplica Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And he's injured, what, as a result of bombing, is he?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was wounded in the village of Kijevo by Siptar terrorist forces. That means not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... just read that entry out so that we can know --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Colonel Trajkovic from Pristina informed the command post of the brigade that soldier Ilic Toplica from the 1st SARD of the anti-aircraft defence was wounded and succumbed to the wounds sustained the previous day. Transferred to the clinical hospital centre in Pristina to collect data."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So this man who subsequently -- who died from earlier wounds, was not actually injured in the course of the Meja campaign, conflict, whatever -- plan, whatever you like to call it, he was injured the previous day, and I think you told us where he was injured. Where was he injured?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wounded 100 kilometres away from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the location of the 1st Artillery Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to the entry that we were looking at, and we can focus on to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one housekeeping matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you said that 26th of April is missing from this war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Am I wrong? Is it included in the original papers? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's included in English translation but I couldn't find the B/C/S version corresponding to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour is absolutely right that we got the transcription for it because it was the fact that we had that, no two following days and the following day, that alerted to me to search for the 27th and 28th. And I think Your Honour is also right that for some reason unexplained by the accused we don't have the original of it. I can't help you with that, that a matter for him. Perhaps he'd further check his own documents and make available the 26th and any other pages he's got.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that if we look at this entry for 600 hours in the morning, this is clearing Siptar terrorist forces under the -- under Reka, and there's a mixed battery of a self-propelled platoon -- is that one of yours?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: An infantry platoon. Is that one of yours, from the logistics battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two infantry battalions. They're yours, are they?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're platoons, not battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two platoons --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One thing at a time.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- from two battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... battalions. It may easily have been a slip of the tongue. Look at the text and tell us what the word is. Is it battalions or platoons?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says platoons from different battalions. From the command artillery battalion and it's actually platoon not battalion. Battalion is the larger unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So what is your unit doing providing -- which is air defence, providing these people for this operation? What were they there to do?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my unit in that operation, although it's not an operation, it's anti-terrorist action, was on the line of blockade that I spoke to you about when I had the map before me. This describes the situation that we saw on that map, and it coincides with this --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- statement of Lieutenant Colonel Odak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. All it describes is "going according to plan, as envisaged." The plan as envisaged is the Reka plan. The Reka plan is something of which we had no knowledge whatsoever until this document was handed over this morning. So in answer to your last observation that this describes what we saw on the map, no, it doesn't. Let's look at the next date because we can --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to say that from this sentence where it says that it's going according to plan, it means that the unit that had received the assignment, my unit, is performing the assignment according to plan, meaning that it's holding the blockade line as envisaged. What is written, what is entered into a war diary are the activities of one's own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course now that we see a number of your units broken down, it will be a very considerable body of contemporaneous material provided, reports up from platoon to whatever the next level after is, company, or company to brigade, plenty of material, all of it stored in the same archive probably as this war diary is stored in. It's all there, isn't it, that contemporaneous material? Isn't it, Mr. Djosan?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Archives are kept in a certain place. The archives of the brigade which I commanded had their own location. Archives of another unit have another location. The corps archives have a third location. Conditionally speaking, they may be in the same building, but to speak of an archives holding all these documents mixed, such a thing does not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I see you're not claiming that any of these archives have been destroyed by NATO bombing, or will you do that now?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who mentioned bombing now? I'm not even saying that my own archives were destroyed during the war, let alone other people's. Please do not put words in my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many -- how many prisoners, by the way, were taken on the 27th? Presumably if it's an operation to do with terrorists, you want prisoners. Where are they, a record of the prisoners? Or was it like Racak again, no prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit did not take a single prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And anybody else --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- prisoner? Tell us, did any other part of the VJ or the MUP or the paramilitaries take a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, paramilitaries -- do I really need to tell you five times that there were no paramilitary units? Would you please accept something when I say it? Second, I don't know what other units did. It's not my responsibility or my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you see --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit did not have any contact --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been very free with secondhand information about whether there were paramilitaries anywhere within Kosovo, and you've told us there weren't. You've had lots of sources of information. When I ask you a question about something rather nearer to home, you plead ignorance. Just yes or no, because we'll eventually perhaps get the records from elsewhere and I don't know what the answer is. I'm going to suggest one but I don't know at the moment because we haven't got all the records. You tell us. Were there any prisoners taken at Meja on the 27th and 28th? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go to the 28th, please, have a look at that. Next page, please, Mr. Nort. And I think but I'm not so sure, but just check, the first entry -- and I'll ask my colleague to check as I'm asking the question to make sure I'm not misunderstanding the position. The first entry and the entries from 1500, 1800 onwards all relate to air defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1800 hours, daily report to the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Okay. But let's -- I think the others are air defence. But let's go back to 0700 then. Perhaps you'd read out the 0700 entry, which I think may be of interest to us. Could you read that out, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Brief agreement reaching meeting between organs of the brigade command for the engagement during the day where the following was emphasised: The intervention unit is still engaged in the Reka action. The engineering and NHB are to scout for alternative routes in case of destruction of the Terup [phoen] bridge and another bridge."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pausing there [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Management of motor vehicles --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "-- only by soldiers envisaged by establishment."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll pick it up from there for the next entry in a second, but what's now clear is that there was a meeting between organs of the brigade command planning for the day. Can you tell me, please, where is the record of that plan and why isn't it here?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's here. This is -- this is the event --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as it was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It doesn't actually set out where anybody is deployed. It doesn't set out what anybody's got to do. It doesn't give a history of what's happened. It simply says then the intervention unit is still engaged in the Reka action. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means what I have been telling you over the past few days, that it was still up there in the same location where it would stay until 1600 hours on this day. And that confirms my statement and the statement by Lieutenant Colonel Odak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And which of the earlier referred units is the intervention platoon, please? We had your account of platoons previously. Which bit is the intervention platoon, or is it something separate?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intervention platoon is a general name for a unit that is established in the event of an attack or danger to certain forces. Every artillery battalion of ours, if it's attacked simultaneously from the ground and from the air, because it had constant engagement in the air, had to repel terrorist attacks. Terrorist attacks by Siptars were a regular occurrence against our artillery battalions when they were fighting NATO forces in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's read the next bit of the entry. Pick it up from where you left it off. And we're about, I think, down to either 0800 or 1500. In fact, probably started at 0800.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Command organs working according to plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Then?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1500 hours: "Commander and the chief of -- chief of operations and training spent time in the 3rd Artillery Battalion of air defence and performed a check of the rocket battery, indicating on the spot a number of omissions and made specific critical comments. Chief of Staff leading intervention unit in the action Reka. Enemy aviation intensively reconnoitering individual and occasionally acts against selected targets."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause there.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At 10.15 they acted --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause there.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "-- against the Devet Jugovica barracks."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What we can see in relation to what was happening in the valley leading down to Meja is that the Chief of Staff -- who's that? Leading --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my deputy, Colonel Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Colonel Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Novica Stankovic. Colonel Novica Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've got some statements in our bundle. Have you produced statements from Stankovic? Have you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask a statement from him but you can get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... bundle, is he?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is he still alive and well, Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where does he live?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any reason why you know that he's not giving or prepared to give, if that's the case, a statement about these events that he commanded?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know any reasons concerning him, but I don't believe he has anything to hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Everybody of potential importance was called in by the commission, but the commission was ultimately dependent, I suppose, to some degree on cooperation. Do you know if this man was called in?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not called.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Everybody knows who has read "As Seen, As Told" or "Under Orders" or the evidence in this case, or countless other accounts of Meja knows that what is alleged is that the army guarded the territory while others did the killing. The man in charge of the intervention platoon would know about that, wouldn't he, whether it's true or false? He'd know it more than you because he was nearer the action.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why not? Why isn't that true? Please tell me. Why have I got that wrong?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not true because, first of all, the army did not secure or provide security to anybody who was killing people. The army and the police in Kosovo and Metohija did not kill people. They were fighting terrorists, just like terrorists are fought everywhere else in the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we have to take the adjournment now. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On volunteers, can we look, please, at what you said. You said that volunteers weren't ever allowed to form a significant part or a whole of a unit. Can we look at an exhibit that's been provided for Vukovic, tab 4A, as we understand it, of his materials. And he reports in 4A the following -- top of the page, please. The passage that's highlighted. We can go through this with Vukovic, but he says there's something called the Phantom Volunteer Platoon in the Zverka squad from the reconnaissance company. What was the Phantom Volunteer Platoon, please, if it wasn't a volunteer platoon?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear about this. And Vukovic was not my officer nor do I know what he said there. I don't know anything about that, so you would have to ask Vukovic that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So your general knowledge of what was happening in Kosovo may be a bit flawed because things may have been happening under your nose or next door to your nose and you wouldn't know what it was, what was happening; is that right? The way you put it was it was impossible to have ten volunteers among a platoon of 30 people, is one of the things you said. Now we seem to have a full platoon.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Can we look at the next document, please, which comes, I think, from Farkas's proposed exhibits, 13A of those.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just respond. I was speaking about my own unit. Colonel Vukovic was not my unit so I cannot speak in his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would it be prudent for us, reviewing your evidence, to shrink everything you've said only to be relevant to your unit and your immediate area of local knowledge? Would that be a prudent course for us to take?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Abso --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I'm testifying here exclusively about knowledge about my unit, its activities and its tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... unfortunate or dishonest when you gave answers that were broad in their apparent compass?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly not dishonest. I came here to tell the truth, and I don't wish to guess and speculate. You expect me to give you half-truths and speculations and I have no intention of doing that nor am I allowed to do that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Djosan, we wouldn't be dealing with these matters if you hadn't chosen, volunteered to make wide-ranging statements about military and other practice in all of Kosovo. This follows from your answers, from nothing else. Let's look at 13A of Farkas, please, on the question of both volunteers and paramilitaries and then we'll look at paramilitaries very briefly. This is a document that's going to be produced, I think, by Farkas as his 13A. Could you lay it on the overhead projector, please, Mr. Nort. And that's fine. Bottom paragraph, "In the initial --" this is a document of the 20th of April, 1999. "In the initial period no processing of volunteers was organised at the Bubanj Potok PC, they were simply rounded up and taken to the 3rd Army PC, often without any agreement or coordination. They mostly belonged to previously formed paramilitary groups, and a number of them were 'unfit' for military service (limping, alcoholics, blind, missing an eye, and so on), and eventually sent back to the 1st Army. A number of volunteers in these groups have a criminal record. In addition, a number --" that's all we need trouble with. Now, this document, of course, purports to show efforts to tidy the position up, but is it right, as Farkas sets out here in dealing with Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the dispatch of volunteers to the 3rd Army, that there were volunteers formed from or mostly formed from paramilitary groups, many of them with criminal records? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Farkas meant here, meant to say here. You have his statement, so you can ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, is it right, because you've given -- I know you're now happy to shrink your evidence to your own locality but we've got to deal with the things you said, however briefly. Is it right that there were people fighting on this territory who started off as criminals, became paramilitaries and were then drafted into the army via the process of being volunteers? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge of that. I know that my volunteers were decent people, honest people and that they were included in our units. Now, as to some other things that were said here, I really couldn't say because it would be just saying what somebody else had already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last point on volunteers in light of your general answers: Are you aware of the Skorpions, the people who it is said killed on the video that's been screened to a very small extent here but rather more fully in Belgrade? Are you aware of the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about them on television. Otherwise, no specific knowledge about them. Anything that I was able to hear on television, that's the extent of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you aware that they were deployed in Kosovo in response to perceived need? Their first action was to go and kill innocent civilians in Podujevo. They were withdrawn, they were re-engaged, and according to the evidence of General Vasiljevic given a couple of years ago at page 15988, when re-engaged, they went and killed 20 civilians in Gnjilane? Were you aware of that? Killing 20 civilians by a paramilitary group, as General Vasiljevic explains it, is pretty important stuff, isn't it? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. You'll have to ask him. If he said that, then I suppose he had some idea for presenting that. I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... about what General Vasiljevic says, about a matter of factual history like that, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have reason to doubt everything that I did not see myself or hear or read.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You heard the question. Feel free to say whatever you like about anybody, because people do in this Court, but you just tell us, do you have any reason to doubt what General Vasiljevic told this Court by way of his evidence? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what all the things are that he said here. Only when I hear what he said can I say whether I have reason to doubt or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to burning of buildings, can you look, please, at this document, the Delic exhibit. This is an exhibit produced via Delic. So -- do you doubt Delic or have any reason to -- it's D299, tab 72. Any reason to doubt General Delic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, let me state again, I doubt everything that I didn't see myself on the spot here and see --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, this is a record of a MUP staff meeting held on the 11th of May of 1999 in Pristina. And if we go to, in the English, page 12 -- can you go to what is chapter or part 12 and go to the very last part of it in the original. Those are paragraph numbers and you come to number 12, which deals with the 124th Brigade, company commander Colic. Do you know him? Do you know Colic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, what it records -- have you got to chapter -- or paragraph 12? Have you found that? Then when you've found it, simply go to the last paragraph of this record of a MUP staff meeting on the 11th of May of 1999, and it says this of Djakovica. It says: "Citizens and refugees in Djakovica town were treated correctly during the operations, however, after all the actions, VJ reservists burnt houses and went into them; we informed VJ commanders in order to prevent these incidents." Well, now, you've told us you were there and how well everybody behaved. Yes or no: Did VJ reservists burn houses, as even recorded in a MUP staff meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend a MUP meeting and I'm not aware of that. General Delic had a much wider area. It was my duty to deal with air defence exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been shrinking down your evidence into what you're familiar with. Just tell us this: Is it possible that houses were burned in Djakovica by military reservists without your knowing about it? Or is the MUP lying about it because they were burning houses and they wanted to blame the VJ? Tell us. There's got to be some reason for this entry.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many houses in Djakovica burnt down. Most of them were burnt after the 24th of March, after the NATO planes had struck. I never saw or heard that reservists, either of the army of Yugoslavia or of the police, set fire to houses, nor do I have knowledge about that from my subordinate officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I possibly repeat the first part of that question, and just listen carefully and please try to answer it directly. Is it possible that houses were burned in Djakovica by military reservists without you knowing about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What about the houses that were burnt before the NATO planes, as you say, struck? Who burnt them down? It wasn't the Albanians burning their own houses, was it? So who burnt those houses down?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I do not have knowledge about that. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You said -- see, it's your answer, Mr. Djosan. We're not tricking you. We're just following your answers. And what you said was most -- many houses in Djakovica burnt down. Most of them were burnt after the 24th of March. So you obviously had in mind, as you were giving that answer, those that were burnt before. Or was it some kind of -- was it some kind of spontaneous combustion or a gas explosion, or negligence in the bedroom, or what was it? With a cigarette. Tell us, what burnt the houses down?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see how -- would you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see how you conclude that I said that. What I said was -- would you repeat what you said from the beginning, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll repeat some of it, not the full extent of the answer, but what you said was, "Many houses in Djakovica burnt down. Most of them were burnt after the 24th of March, after the NATO planes had struck." If you say most of something happened afterwards, the clear inference is that the balance happened before, and I just want to know how those houses that burnt --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I said was that many houses and most of the houses. Not all the houses in Djakovica were burnt. Had I said that all the houses in Djakovica had burnt down and that many had been burnt after the 24th of March, then you could infer and conclude what you're doing. But many houses burnt after the 24th of March, many of them remained standing. So that is how I interpret my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I wonder if that's reasonable. Maybe there's a translation problem here, but it's not been suggested to you that all the houses in Djakovica were burned down. The point that you're being asked about is saying that most of the ones that were burned were burned after the 24th, and the question you're then asked is what caused the burning of the houses which were burned before the 24th? Now, could you deal with that directly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. I don't know that the houses were burned before that, before the 24th of March. I'm not aware of that. I did not receive any report about that. I didn't see a single house burning before the 24th of March. I don't know about it -- that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So in other words, your previous answer was wrong. Was that a slip of the tongue or a mistake or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood you to -- or, rather, when I said that many houses burned after the 24th of March, I didn't mean to imply that some of them had been burnt before the 24th of March. I just said that many remained standing, not -- had not been set fire to, had not been burning and so on, had not burnt and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On bombing and your maps, I don't have time to go through them, but just these two points: Have you read and considered at all the report of -- the expert report of a man called Patrick Ball about the correlation of bombing and movement of refugees?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He said when -- there is no correlation between changes in bombing rate and changes in refugee flow. I take it that since you have haven't read it you have no way of countering his arguments, obviously. And when we look at your maps, there is no statistics for the dates of bombs, is there, really? There's no detail on any of your maps for the dates of bombs.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of those places are authentic. On that map you cannot introduce each individual specific piece of detail. I claim that on certain maps, and specifically on the map that I showed you of the 2nd infantry battalion, that each place corresponds to the NATO Air Force targets. If we were to show all the targets on Kosovo and Metohija, you would need a map the size of one square kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... small bomb, it could be a big bomb, it could be a bomb that had a frightening effect, it could be a bomb that had a surgically defined target and might have a less frightening effect. Do you accept those propositions?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if I was to suggest to you that the majority of people had already left by the time the majority of the bombing started, are you in a position to counter that, or do you accept that? A large amount of the population movement happened before the bombing was at its worst in this area. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by the largest amount or greatest phase, most intensive phase. The first bomb that fell unleashed the movement of refugees. Individuals left -- some left straight away. Others expected it to last only briefly and stayed on. But as the aggression or, rather, the interval of the bombings intensified -- as the bombing rate intensified, the number of refugees increased. So throughout the aggression, the whole of the NATO aggression, there were refugees. Some stayed put for longer periods of time, others for shorter periods. I didn't say that all the refugees left the same day. But there was refugee movement throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- Mr. Djosan, that there was no flight of refugees before the bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the bombing on the 24th of March, they did not leave in the sense of -- they did not exit in the sense of going to Albania. Yes, there were movements from the places where there was a conflict and clash between the army of Yugoslavia and MUP on the one side with the terrorists on the other. People did leave there, but not en masse. There wasn't a massive movement of refugees until the NATO strikes started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Crime and punishment. You've produced one document, I think, dealing with allegations of rape. I'm not going to go into that. I don't have time. Is there any evidence of any soldier charged in respect of either something like burning someone's house to drive them out of the area or killing people in order to kill them and drive out others? Is there any allegation like that contained -- sorry, any record of anything like that anywhere, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, I have detailed information about my own soldiers. However, as I didn't have the police and that -- or -- and that -- or I can't tell you specifically about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the judiciary that was working. There were criminal reports filed. There were criminal reports coming from my unit, too, and I assumed that if the rest of the commanders had cases like that, they would report them. But all I can talk about is my own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're aware, though, aren't you, that there's either no or almost no records anywhere in Kosovo about people being pursued for their destruction or the killing that constitute ethnic cleansing? No records of any such inquiries.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it wasn't ethnic cleansing of any kind; and secondly, I have information pertaining to my soldiers alone, those whom I turned over to the military courts. So I can't talk about other units. I don't know what happened there. How would you expect me to know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Obviously it's for the learned Court in due course to decide whether there was ethnic cleansing or not, but what is clear is that if there was ethnic cleansing, there was no effort made to root out the people who were doing it or to prosecute them. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ethnic cleansing exists. It exists today in Kosovo and Metohija, now. That is when ethnic cleansing is taking part. Kosovo and Metohija is really ethnically clear now. And you know who is in Kosovo and Metohija now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I understand your question, although I'm not going to answer it, which brings me usefully to my penultimate topic, very briefly, the VJ commission again. Are you one of those Serbs who would say that Kosovo Albanians will say whatever they are expected to say if they're approached by us, to lie and all that sort thing? Is that your attitude to Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider that to be true about individual witnesses who are under threat. I didn't say that all of them would, and I never tend to generalise. So I can't -- just like I didn't speak about other soldiers from other units, I can't make a sweeping statement about all Albanians either. It is to be expected that most witnesses under pressure would be prepared to say a lot, but I didn't say all. How should I know that all, everybody would do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, on a proper analysis of what's happened in Kosovo, the following emerges, doesn't it: In military and political terms, the KLA's won and the Serbs have been defeated and driven away. We express, obviously, no opinion one way or another as to whether it's a good or bad thing, that's just a fact. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where do you get that idea from, that the KLA can win over the regular army of a country? How can you say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you don't accept the proposition, I'll move on. But the KLA - would you accept this - are now in an environment where they certainly have nothing to fear -- not that they have nothing to fear but they don't have much to fear from Serbs because there aren't very many Serbs there and because Kosovo Albanians run their own country. Well, not their own country, they run Kosovo, whatever it is, I'm not going to express an opinion on that either.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kosovo Albanians now do not run Kosovo themselves, just as the Serbs do not run Kosovo and Metohija themselves either. We know full well who it is that is running Kosovo and Metohija and how that came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Serbs from Kosovo, such as you, in Belgrade are actually under Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. enormous pressure when organised, to use a neutral term, by something like the VJ Commission for Cooperation, aren't you? You're under enormous pressure, all of you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "under enormous pressure."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What enormous pressure?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Having lost, having failed to hold Kosovo despite grave criminality, you're now at risk of being exposed, all of you, for the crimes you've committed, and that's why you have to hang together. And that's what we are seeing in your evidence and in these documents you produce -- produced years after the event. You and most of your colleagues are hanging together.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where do you get that idea from? I think that that is an insult to this Court, and I'm not going to listen to any political propaganda here. I don't know whose positions you are an advocate of, but from what you've just said, I could conclude that you were very, very close to helping and assisting the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You remember that you had no observations adverse to General Vasiljevic. You said you couldn't, of course, express an opinion on him, on his evidence, without reviewing it all. Fair enough. Nevertheless , you know nothing adverse to him.
