Can you think of any good reason why this commission through whom you have been operating to bring evidence should attempt to put him off from giving evidence, should attempt to restrict his access to the Office of the Prosecution until he had the courage to make his own communication? Can you think of any reason why the commission should intervene with a person like that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't wish to think about General Vasiljevic at all. Why should I? They're his affairs, his business what he thinks and what he's going to say, where and when. It's up to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I know? I don't actually know him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last question, different topic. You were in Djakovica from, on any reckoning, mid-1998. I'm going to ask you to look at a document that's already been exhibited in this case. It's Exhibit 667, tab 35. Let me tell you about the document while it's being distributed. It's a stenographically recorded record of something called the Supreme Defence Council. It was produced by the authorities of Serbia and Montenegro. It's accuracy has thus far never been challenged, and it sets out what various high-ranking people said, word for word. The passage that I'm going to ask you to look at comes from a meeting held on the 13th of April, 1995, and it relates to Djakovica, which is why I'm asking you about it. Now, if you have the page in front you, and we can put the English page 20 -- page 24 like that, Mr. Nort. Thank you. A bit further down the page. And you'll be found it by Mr. Nort. Give it a little context. Give it a little context. The accused, Slobodan Milosevic, is recorded as saying, in a discussion with Perisic and Lilic: "... 'first 15 days of terrorist ...' and you act with 130.000. You don't act with 130.000 ... you have additional 100.000 police forces that will act in terrorist and other situations, special police units - they will act together with the Army." Well, this is 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, could you speak down a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm so sorry. My mistake. I'll read it again. He speaks of acting with 130.000 people. "... you have additional 100.000 police forces that will act in terrorist and other situations, special police units - that will act together with the Army." Now, this is 1995. You were there in 1998 but you must have learnt something of the history. Is it right that there were 100.000 police force available?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then let's look over to what General Perisic said. He said, "Fine. I thought I was not in charge of proposing all that." The accused says: "Yes, I understand. But all this must be inter-related. For example, the most beautiful town in Kosovo, the one in which the Siptar separatists invested the most, that is the Djakovica group, is Djakovica. There is no prettier, richer, or more organised town in Kosovo than Djakovica is. It is situated in the most beautiful place, and there is a former barracks a bit uphill, currently abandoned." Well, let's deal with his description of Djakovica. Is he being genuine or is he being ironic? Is it in fact a beautiful place? You tell us. Or was it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djakovica used to be a beautiful town, and the living was good in Djakovica, and this hill that is mentioned here is a beautiful hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then the accused goes on to say: "There is a former barracks and an armoured motorised unit should be relocated there so that they know that their treasure will be under attack tomorrow is something that must not and need not start happening. They need to know that the army exists and that it is there." Perisic says: "We have a barracks there."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SAYS
utterances.text: "You have nothing there." Perisic: "I have a battalion there."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "No, you don't, you have an empty barracks." Next page, please. Perisic: "What kind of chief of the general staff would I be if I didn't know that, Mr. President? I have a battalion at Djakovica at the exit Dzapa Prusica on the left side. I've been there three times."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "What is up with that barracks uphill Djakovica? Why is it abandoned?" "It's been abandoned for a long time now." "I don't mean that you abandoned it," says the accused, "I'm saying it's been abandoned for a long time." Perisic: "Someone has deserted it. I don't know why. Every town in Kosovo has a barracks and an army. I don't have enough soldiers." Now, before we read the last passage, is it right that there was a deserted barracks and was it filled between 1995 and 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: My late father Miko, in 1932 served in the army in Djakovica. He did his military service there in the barracks that was called 156th Iron Regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just answer the question and leave aside the anecdote.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was an abandoned barracks there, a deserted barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it filled, was it reoccupied between 1995 and 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A brigade of air defence arrived, that I commanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exactly. So that when we see the accused saying they, the occupants of this beautiful place, need to know that the army exists and that it is there, it was you, amongst others, who fulfilled that part of his objective. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do your beautiful towns not have an army barracks? The air defence unit of which I was commander had the task, because since 1996 pilotless aircraft had started to appear in our airspace and it was quite obvious they were not there to spy on Italy. It was quite normal for an air defence unit to occupy that place to provide observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware that Perisic hadn't been in favour of it and that it was this accused's intention, certainly in 1995, to cause a visible armed presence to loom over Djakovica town?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That air defence unit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear what the witness said. It was drowned by another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The -- please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said is the air defence unit is not really invisible. It's a brigade. Second, how could I know the thinking of General Perisic? Even if I knew something about it, it was not mine to question it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's read the very last passage of this accused on this topic. He said the following: "Kosovo is our safest territory." Remember, Mr. Djosan, these are his stenographically recorded words. "We sent 9.000 students there to study at the Pristina University; the Serbian daughters who are their parents' only child, can walk alone in Pristina in the middle of the night. They figured out that it was not a good thing to do, they saw what happened in Bosnia. But it is good to have it there, that you have them there and that it's function -- that is functioning. It is well known that 'Fear keeps the house safe.'" Possibly "Fear guards the house." Maybe the interpreters would be good enough to interpret for us the words which appear in --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I had those papers that you were reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. The last part of the passage. Yes. He's describing the reality of life in Kosovo in 1995. Peaceful, safe on the streets, but nevertheless desirable to put places like Djakovica under fear of the military, because fear guards the house. And I invite the interpreters, if they have the original, which they can find on page 26, to read so that we can have an interpretation of what appears to be a quotation. I thought I'd tracked it down once but I haven't at this time. "Strah, kucu, cuva"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Safeguards, keeps it safe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army of Yugoslavia never had the intention or the task to intimidate its own population. Why would it? Those were our citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... placed there to intimidate it when it wanted to take revenge, as it did following the death of a policeman, himself almost certainly a war criminal, I must suggest to you. You, and you know this, guarded not the house but you guarded the MUP while they went down and butchered people in Meja. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are your insinuations and maybe wishes, maybe wishful thinking on your part, but certainly insinuations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Milosevic, any re-examination? If there is, let it be short and to the point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice raised certain things in cross-examination here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead. Just remember, it's not everything that Mr. Nice raises that requires an answer from you in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said, Mr. Robinson, I will be brief and concise, but there are certain points raised by Mr. Nice in cross-examination that I cannot overlook. Of course I never intended to respond to all of them. He raised even some new issues, though, and twisted others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, at the very beginning Mr. Nice asked you some questions related to your activities year by year in your career and place of service.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, you explained that you were in the army of Serbian Krajina from the 1st of January, until the 30th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, General, who sent you there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the Serbian army of Krajina at my own personal request through the 40th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned, although in passing, without any questions from Mr. Nice on that topic, that you did not receive special allowance for living apart from your family. In fact, you said, "While I was in Pristina, I had this allowance for separation from my family but not in Krajina." Please explain. Who receives this allowance for separation from family and how does it work?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This allowance is given to members of the army of Yugoslavia who work in garrisons which do not house their families. For instance, I was in Pristina while my family was in Belgrade, and based on the costs that I incurred because of living apart from my family, I received an allowance. That is an allowance that an officer receives when he lives away from the place where he has a flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that apply to all members of the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you were in the army of Serbian Krajina as a volunteer, was your family with you in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did not you -- why didn't you then receive that allowance then?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't entitled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why weren't you entitled?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The state did not pay that allowance to people who volunteered to go to the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please observe a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say a moment ago that all members of the army receive allowance for living away from their family when they go to work in other garrisons?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If they go there following orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So why didn't you receive it then?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was not following orders to go there. I went there at my own request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During that time, were you considered to be a member of the army of Yugoslavia or a member of the Serbian army of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the Serbian army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nice asked you about the exhumation of bodies in Batajnica, linking it several times to your service in Batajnica. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That location where you served in Batajnica, is it in any way related to the place where the bodies were exhumed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In no way whatsoever. I served at the Batajnica airport. At the end of the runway there was the position of the rocket battalion SAM 3, and that was our position. So I served at Batajnica airport, air field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the incident where bodies were exhumed, you said it was preposterous that something like that could happen during the war, that it took you three days to travel in a passenger vehicle from Djakovica to Belgrade to visit your family. You said it is highly improbable for something like that to happen during the war. Is it more probable in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice told you that it is well known to you that Albanians were not welcome in Serbia. Do you know how many Albanians live in Belgrade and in other areas of Serbia outside Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade, from what I know, there are 100.000 Albanians residing. I don't have exact information, I could not give you the exact figure, but it is a large number of Albanians who live in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Have you ever heard that any --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... but I certainly have no recollection of saying that and it may be that something's been either considered out of context or whatever, but I stand to be corrected but I don't think I've ever said anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I myself don't recall that, Mr. Milosevic. Can you put it in context as to whether --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript is there to jog our memories. Mr. Nice said that when he was questioning the witness to the effect that how could the Albanians have effected this manipulation when they were not welcome in Serbia. So I asked the witness is it true that Albanians were not welcome in Serbia and how many of them were actually living outside Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General Djosan, have you ever heard of any Albanian in Belgrade suffering in an incident, even during the war in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of an Albanian business in Belgrade having their shop windows shattered or something like that? And I suppose you would be able to see that because you walk the streets all the time.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. They have their businesses in best locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see from the shops and the inscriptions on top that they are owned by Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice asked you something about the evidence given by Nik Peraj, who was your subordinate. He asked you about his character, whether he was an honest man, whether he had any reason to lie. He wanted your answers. Please try to remember, did I ask you about the character of Nik Peraj during my examination or did I ask you about facts?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: About facts only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So if he speaks in three occasions about a brigade from Republika Srpska in Djakovica, is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So can you say in answer to that that that's something untrue or it's something unbalanced?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a fact, because I cooperated with SFOR in Djakovica, and it was not possible for a single soldier, let alone an armoured brigade, to come in from Republika Srpska. It is complete ignorance, untruth. Call it what you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, I was questioning you about facts, not about the character of Nik Peraj. If he says that you arrested Micunovic, does it have to do with character or fact when you say, "I never arrested him or had anything to do with him"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does relate to character, because he's lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, character is always at issue in cross-examination. Second, as a matter of fact, the accused asked the question. He may not have expected the answer he got, but he did ask the question about the honesty of Mr. Peraj to this witness, and got an answer saying that Mr. Peraj was, so far as he knew at the time, honest. And so I'm not quite sure where these questions are really going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm not sure myself where the questions are leading. It's matter for us to determine credibility.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice tried to rehabilitate the evidence given by his witness Nik Peraj, whereas in a number of points that have to do with factual information, General Djosan responded it was completely untrue. Such as the VRS brigade in Djakovica, the arrest of Micunovic, paramilitary units. It is a string of facts given in evidence by Nik Peraj and challenged --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- emphatically by General Djosan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The evidence is there for us to analyse, and you can address us on that at the appropriate time, not now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I wanted to point out that General Djosan contested the facts as alleged by Nik Peraj, whereas Mr. Nice wanted to rehabilitate Nik Peraj by asking whether he was an honest man, whether something was balanced or unbalanced, whether he had any reason to lie, et cetera, whereas notorious lies were put forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We've heard a comment. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So if Nik Peraj said that your officer, Major Winter, had written a report to the staff of the 3rd Army, saying that terrorists had been killed in Meja, was he telling the truth or lying?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will not dwell on Nik Peraj any more because he doesn't deserve it, but I will dwell on something else. Mr. Nice asked you several times from different aspects why you believed that Albanian witnesses were under pressure. Do you remember him asking you that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I will read out to you now just a brief quotation of an answer from Mr. Nice's side to a request that has to do with Ramush Haradinaj. So it's the same party that claims that Albanians are not under pressure there. In --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- point 7 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... another case, apparently. Something said by someone else in another case, I suspect. I don't see how it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in order to ensure that the hearing scheduled this afternoon begins on time, we are going to stop at 1.43.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Just this brief quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's an official submission of the party represented here by Mr. Nice to a Trial Chamber, Judge Agius, Eser, and Brydensholt, and in point 7, it says: "Kosovo is still a very violent region." Volatile, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, stop. Let us be told what it is that you're referring to. I don't know what it is that you're referring to. A submission by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am referring to a submission filed by Stefan Waespi, trial attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, I see, filed by an officer of the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. It's their submission. And in that submission, dated 13th October, 2005 - and today we're not far from that - it says: "Kosovo is still a very volatile region. Victims and witnesses have regularly contacted the Prosecution to express their alarm [In English] at the provisional release of this accused --" [Interpretation] they mean Haradinaj -- "[In English] prospective release of any of the other accused. The decision to ease the stringency of the conditions imposed on the accused's provisional release will only accentuate the victims' and witnesses' anxieties."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So can we see from this that the party represented here by Mr. Nice is very well aware why Albanian witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- are upset?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... this material. If the accused wants to press on with it, or if the Court was even minded to let him press on with it, it's got to recognise that what is being talked about there is Kosovo Albanians giving evidence in cases of Kosovo Albanian accused. Arguably different, as we know the way things have changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is not a fruitful area of inquiry. A question like that can't be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I get it wrong or did you explain that Albanians in this situation have to testify, as expected by the KLA, fearing from their -- for their own lives or for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fearing for their own lives and for the lives of their dearest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Responding to Mr. Nice, you raised a completely new topic that I did not cover in my examination-in-chief, namely that you headed the commission for the application for -- of the Military Technical Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that while explaining why you believed that the representatives on the location were not objective vis-a-vis the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You started by saying that a mass grave was uncovered, that a Serb body was found, and then at the request of one of those representatives, the mass grave was immediately closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As I indicated --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- we have to adjourn at 1.43, which is now, and we will resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of October, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
